title: Goldwyn Bets on French WW2 Epic ‘De Gaulle’ Crossing Over to U.S. Audiences: ‘It’s the Story of an Ally’
description: Antonin Baudry’s two-part World War II epic about Charles de Gaulle made its U.S. premiere Saturday at the American French Film Festival in Los Ang
body:
Antonin Baudry’s two-part World War II epic about Charles de Gaulle made its U.S. premiere Saturday at the American French Film Festival in Los Angeles, drawing a seven-minute standing ovation after both installments, each running more than two and a half hours, played back-to-back to packed audiences at the DGA Theater.

	The €74 million production, starring Simon Abkarian as the French general and Simon Russell Beale as Winston Churchill, marks one of Pathé’s boldest gambles following “The Count of Monte Cristo” and the two-part “The Three Musketeers,” which were also distributed in the U.S. by Samuel Goldwyn Films.
	

	After a slow start in France, the films quietly gained momentum through word of mouth, becoming a domestic box office success and selling over six million tickets, and are now gaining traction internationally. In the U.K., the first installment, “De Gaulle: Resistance,” which charts De Gaulle’s heroic battle to build a Resistance movement after France surrendered to Nazi Germany in 1940, currently ranks as the highest-grossing French-language film of the year. “De Gaulle” has also just been acquired in China – a rare feat — where Light Films will release it in late November.

	In the U.S., Goldwyn is rolling out the epic theatrically across major U.S. markets, including New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, San Francisco, Washington, D.C., Seattle, Austin, Minneapolis, Houston and Atlanta, while making it available nationwide on transactional VOD. The second film, “De Gaulle: Liberty” will be released in early December.

	Speaking to Variety during the American French Film Festival, Peter Goldwyn said he’s betting that the sprawling saga can appeal to U.S. audiences even if it revolves around a French historical figure that many aren’t familiar with.
	

	“The films have proven themselves, and audiences are audiences, whether they’re American or French,” Goldwyn said. “It’s an amazing feat of filmmaking that you don’t quite see anymore and ultimately, World War II is an easy entry point for U.S. audiences.”

	“U.S. audiences have been very much enthusiastic consistently about stories about Roosevelt, about Churchill, and I think that the story of De Gaulle is relatively untold in America,” he continued, adding that the “staggering scope and scale of what (De Gaulle) accomplished as one man is pretty amazing.”

	Goldwyn argued that the films’ cinematic ambition places them closer to Hollywood blockbusters than conventional European arthouse fare.

	“As a film itself, you’re looking at something on the scale of ‘The Odyssey.’ It’s just really broad and massive, and yet instead of getting lost in the effects and the war itself, it really does come down to a character study which drives the story along. So you’re not just sitting there watching World War II play out,” he said.

	“The only thing that makes it an arthouse movie is because it’s in a foreign language,” he added, pointing out that the French language “makes it hard for theaters to commit on that wide of a screen count.”

	As such, Goldwyn opted to pair the theatrical run with a nationwide transactional VOD release, giving the films the best chance of finding their audience. 

	“In France it had this sort of slow start and was really discovered, but theaters in the U.S. don’t have the patience or time to let things be discovered. It’s sort of you’re in and you’re out,” he said. “So it’s a combination method.”

	The distributor is mounting a single campaign for both installments, targeting not only arthouse moviegoers but also history buffs, schools, cultural institutions and younger audiences through social media. “I think it’s enhancement, especially when you have two movies of this length, you need word of mouth and if you can only have a couple showtimes a day, you can only get so many people into the theaters,” Goldwyn said.

	The appeal of the films also lies in the fact that they challenge the familiar American and British narratives of World War II, exposing the tensions between De Gaulle, Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt, played by Campbell Scott.
	

	Baudry and his co-screenwriter, Bérénice Vila, read more than 150 books and dug into historical archives to reconstruct the general’s extraordinary journey from an isolated, virtually unknown military officer in 1940 to the leader of the French Resistance, as well as his relationship with Churchill and Roosevelt.

	“They had different conceptions of war. Roosevelt, for his part, thought Churchill was being completely absurd with his romantic ideas about supporting this admirable little leader called De Gaulle. To Roosevelt, the idea of Free France was a little fantasy of Churchill’s,” said Baudry.

	The director said the complicated relationship among the three leaders remains largely unknown outside academic circles.

	“All of this history has never really been told. Historians, real historians who research this period and have access to the sources, know all of this, but the general public doesn’t. And the version of history taught in schools is not very complete,” he said.

	Despite the historical complexity, Baudry wanted the films to be accessible to viewers with no knowledge of De Gaulle, so he organized early screenings for young students outside academic circles.

	“My goal was that you could watch the film without any outside references, without ever having heard of that period or of De Gaulle,” he said.

	One of Baudry’s boldest choices was casting Abkarian, a renowned actor with a career in film and theater who isn’t a bankable star, to embody the towering historical figure.

	Abkarian spent roughly six months preparing for the role of De Gaulle, whose rigid posture, distinctive voice and almost eccentric behavior have long made him difficult to portray.

	“I read the screenplay more than ten times. I read it and reread it and annotated things,” Abkarian told Variety. “There was nothing to change in the writing, not even a comma. The dialogue was really well written.”

	The iconic monologues came more naturally. “There were the great speeches, and that’s where I feel at home because I come from the theater and I know how to approach them.”

	Abkarian also transcribed every line of his dialogue into a small notebook that he carried throughout the 150-day shoot and eventually gave to Baudry.
	

	“All the dialogue went right up to the very last page. I hadn’t planned it that way, but every page was filled. I didn’t have to use another notebook,” he said.

	But the actor eventually abandoned the idea of simply reproducing De Gaulle’s mannerisms. “You can’t represent a character like this in a strictly anthropological way. You can invoke him, evoke him, but you can’t actually become him. And it wouldn’t make sense to try,” he said.

	One breakthrough came when Abkarian and Baudry spent an evening recording De Gaulle’s speeches together.

	“We explored how far I could go in approaching his voice, its frequency, its musicality and the way he emphasized certain words that wouldn’t naturally occur to you. I had to understand his logic, the way he articulated his thoughts through language,” Abkarian said. “I couldn’t make him speak in the ordinary, conversational way I’m speaking to you now. Between doing nothing and caricature, I had to find the right balance.”

	The screenplay portrays Churchill and De Gaulle as unlikely allies bound by mutual admiration despite their frequent clashes, and Abkarian found an easy partner in Russell Beale.

	“Simon is an incredible actor who has a profound understanding of great texts, and we have the same approach to the craft,” Abkarian said. “The writing provides such rich material for the actors, particularly for De Gaulle and Churchill.”

	For Abkarian, Churchill and De Gaulle were united by an idealism that set them apart from Roosevelt’s political pragmatism.

	“Churchill and De Gaulle were romantics. They recognized that quality in each other. That’s why they developed that friendship,” he said. “And that’s what makes their relationship beautiful, as well as mad and contradictory.”

	Abkarian is less certain than Goldwyn about how Americans will respond to the films’ portrayal of their wartime leadership, but he believes De Gaulle’s defiance could strike a chord, particularly in today’s political climate.

	“There may be something in De Gaulle’s struggle that speaks to Americans’ own battles, to their sense of nobility and their democratic convictions,” he said. “I think that, from that point of view, Americans could recognize themselves in the Gaullist struggle.”
	

	Goldwyn, for his part, sees a hero Americans will recognize. “It’s a story of an ally,” Goldwyn said. “This man was very patriotic, which I think is very American. He didn’t go along with what his government dictated and said, ‘I don’t believe this, I need to fight for my country.’”

schema.headline: Goldwyn Bets on French WW2 Epic ‘De Gaulle’ Crossing Over to U.S. Audiences: ‘It’s the Story of an Ally’

title: China Box Office: ‘Traces of Justice’ Reclaims Top Spot as Local Debuts ‘Embers’ and ‘The Coffin Swap’ Arrive
description: New Classics Pictures’ crime procedural drama “Traces of Justice” rebounded to first place at the mainland China box office during the Nov. 6–8 wee
body:
New Classics Pictures’ crime procedural drama “Traces of Justice” rebounded to first place at the mainland China box office during the Nov. 6–8 weekend, collecting RMB21.5 million ($3.2 million) over the three-day frame, according to data from Artisan Gateway. 

	The performance lifted the multi-decade investigation epic to $103.7 million since its Oct. 1 release. Directed by Chen Sicheng (“Detective Chinatown”) and co-written with Zhang Ji and Yan Zijie, the drama stars Zhang Yi, Ma Li, and Chen Minghao alongside Karry Wang, Fan Chengcheng, and Chen Feiyu in a narrative tracking an elite public security detective solving complex historical cases based on real events.
	

	Constantin Film and Sony Pictures’ horror reboot “Resident Evil” moved to second position after a month-long reign atop the charts, taking in $3 million in its fifth weekend. The video game adaptation has now reached a cumulative haul of $76 million since launching during the Golden Week corridor on Oct. 5. 

	Tencent Penguin Pictures’ road drama “Embers” debuted in third place, grossing $2.1 million across its two-day opening frame following a Saturday, November 7 rollout. Written and directed by Sun Aoqian, the film stars Song Jia as a weary crematorium worker who accidentally mixes up two sets of funeral ashes. When the families refuse to switch them back, she partners with the deceased’s daughter, played by Vicky Chen, on a journey across the country to return the remains. The cast also features Zu Feng.

	Shanghai Captain’s rural black comedy-thriller “The Coffin Swap” opened in fourth position, pulling in $1.7 million over its two-day weekend debut. Directed by He Nian from a script by Chen Lu, the feature re-adapts Xin Yukun’s 2014 mystery classic “Deep in the Heart” through the lens of He’s acclaimed stage production. Starring Jiang Wu, Du Guangyi, Gu Xin, Fan Yilin, and Wang Weishuai, the narrative unfolds in a secluded village thrown into chaotic intrigue and conflicting cover-ups after an unidentified charred body is discovered.
	

	Beijing Joy Fun Pictures’ body-swap comedy “Mr. & Mrs. Pardon” rounded out the top five, adding $1.4 million in its sixth weekend to lift its cumulative gross to $61.3 million. Directed by Shen Chunyang and written by Ma Duo, the satirical feature stars real-life comedic pair Shen Chunyang and Xiao Shenyang alongside Jia Bing and Yu Yang as an uninspired middle-aged couple forced to navigate marital strain after swapping bodies.

	Mainland China’s overall weekend box office contracted to $16.4 million amid an ongoing fall lull. The 2026 year-to-date box office reached $4.75 billion, trailing the same period in 2025 by 29%.

schema.headline: China Box Office: ‘Traces of Justice’ Reclaims Top Spot as Local Debuts ‘Embers’ and ‘The Coffin Swap’ Arrive

title: ‘Love Is Blind’ Creator on Protecting the Cast and Why He Chose to Keep Rob’s Attack on Production in the Final Cut
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for Season 11 of “Love Is Blind,” including the reunion, now streaming on Netflix.

	Another season of “
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for Season 11 of “Love Is Blind,” including the reunion, now streaming on Netflix.

	Another season of “Love Is Blind” has wrapped up. The Season 11 reunion dropped on Netflix on Sunday, revealing that the one couple who did say “I do” on their wedding day, Sarah Williams and John Shannon, called it quits after he was caught texting with an escort.


	However, the most dramatic part of the season centered on Rob Feeley and Michaella Giorgio, a couple whose relationship exploded in the weeks leading up to their wedding. The messiness began when the pair went out with his friends; after one of the belligerent boys got cut off by the bartender, Feeley then broke the fourth wall and yelled at production to “cut the cameras,” saying, “You’re cut off, I’m cut off.” He started yelling, “I’m not this phony ass Hollywood bullshit.”
	

	“Love Is Blind” creator and CEO of Kinetic Content, Chris Coelen, breaks down the scene below and explains why he decided to keep it in the show.

	“The participants are not under our control. Some shows are produced in what they call a bubble, where the participants are really in a specific location, and they’re with you 24 hours a day. That is not the case on this particular show. So when we are with them, which is not all the time, obviously we look out for them like we would for anyone, and we document their choices,” explains Coelen. “They’re adults, and they’re making their own choices, and we’re there to follow that. I think what you see pretty clearly in that scene is that the bar doesn’t want to serve Rob’s friend anymore; that’s a choice that the bar made, which I wholly agree with.”
	

	He adds that there’s obviously a great deal of editing in the show, since you’re putting days of content into one episode, “but I think we’ve always made the commitment to show the essence of their journeys in an accurate way, and I think that certainly showed who Rob was in that moment in a very accurate way.”

	After the episode aired, many viewers online feared for Giorgio’s safety, something she tells Variety was never a concern.

	“There was never a moment during filming or production where I felt physically unsafe. I also feel very secure in the fact that if I did, I could always speak with production about it,” Giorgio says. “I’m not shy about the things that I need or standing up for myself, so my choices to leave with Rob were 100% mine, and there was never a moment where I felt like he would be physical with me.”

	In fact, after the bar, the group stayed out until the middle of the night. So the next day, it was time for the St. Patrick’s Day pod squad mixer, which only made matters worse; Feeley had a “crash out” (his words), yelling that the whole experience was fake, claiming he was going to be edited poorly and that no one there really cared about him. It ultimately led Giorgio to call off their engagement.

	“Our obligation is always just to support them in whatever they believe. Nobody is ever required to participate in the experience. They are welcome, and we see it happen every season, all the time — people drop out,” says Coelen. “Rob saying, ‘Oh, this is Hollywood bullshit,’ well, it’s his choice. The next day, Michaella was saying, ‘I don’t want to go to this group event.’ They don’t have to go. Nobody’s forcing them to go to the group event. It’s his choice to participate. Our approach is to try to provide the scaffolding for the experience, and then they navigate through that. That’s what’s fascinating to me and what makes every single season unique. Everyone navigates through that in their own particular way.”



	

	



	Seasons 10 and 11 only featured one couple getting married, and, as noted, this season’s didn’t last. However, Giorgio says at the reunion that she still feels like the experiment worked because she did find love. Coelen agrees.

	“It doesn’t worry me at all. The success of a particular season is not based on how many people end up getting married or staying married or getting engaged,” he says. “They get engaged ostensibly because they’re in love. That’s extraordinary. But that’s not where it stops. The true test of ‘Love Is Blind’ is with the love that they formed: Is that capable of surviving the real world?”
	

	He’s also proud that the show has continued to avoid just showing “cookie-cutter” love stories like other dating reality shows do; this season highlighted real challenges and differences between the couples, including Williams and Shannon’s discussions around vaccines and women’s rights. The edit stays neutral, showing both opinions.

	“What I’m really proud of is, we don’t take a position on any of that. Our job is to be a reflection of these particular people’s journeys, and in doing that, I think we’re a really interesting mirror into the society as a whole,” says Coelen. “Going back to Season 1, and moving forward, you can really feel some of the currents in our culture in terms of the things that matter to the participants in making the biggest choice in their life.”

schema.headline: ‘Love Is Blind’ Creator on Protecting the Cast and Why He Chose to Keep Rob’s Attack on Production in the Final Cut

title: Taiwan and South Korea Join Forces on Musical Theater Co-Productions
description: The Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) and the Korean Association of Musical Producers (KAMP) signed a memorandum of understanding at the Taiw
body:
The Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) and the Korean Association of Musical Producers (KAMP) signed a memorandum of understanding at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei to expand musical theater collaboration between Taiwan and South Korea and open up new opportunities across Asia. 

	TAICCA, the Ministry of Culture-backed body that promotes Taiwan’s content industries, organizes the festival.


	The agreement centers on Taiwan–Korea co-productions and industry exchange, with the two organizations aiming to link creators, performers and companies in both markets. It also seeks to encourage cross-border projects and help musicals from both countries reach audiences beyond their home markets.
	

	“Through this collaboration between Taiwan and Korea, we hope to develop new stories together, realize a shared vision of mutual benefit and share our expertise across market boundaries,” said Erica Wang, CEO of TAICCA.

	KAMP President Han Seung-won said he was pleased to witness an important moment in Taiwan–Korea musical theater collaboration. “I believe closer cooperation between Taiwan and Korea can open up a larger market and new business opportunities,” he said.

	Choi Seok-cheol, representative director of the Gimhae Cultural and Tourism Foundation, based in the South Korean city of Gimhae, attended the ceremony as a witness to the signing.

	The agreement builds on TAICCA’s KonTact Taiwan–Korea Musical Co-Development Program, which launched this year with South Korea as its main partner market. The program is designed to help Taiwan’s musical theater industry find international partners and move joint projects forward faster.
	

	TAICCA said the program and the new agreement are meant to strengthen professional networks between the two countries and help grow Asia’s musical theater industry as a whole.

schema.headline: Taiwan and South Korea Join Forces on Musical Theater Co-Productions

title: ‘Gangs of London’ Director Kim Hong-sun Shoots Korean Martial Arts Action Film ‘The Hit List’ With Jung Woo-sung, ‘Squid Game’ Star Wi Ha-jun
description: Kim Hong-sun, the Korean director of “Project Wolf Hunting” and Season 3 of British crime drama “Gangs of London,” is shooting “The Hit List,” a ma
body:
Kim Hong-sun, the Korean director of “Project Wolf Hunting” and Season 3 of British crime drama “Gangs of London,” is shooting “The Hit List,” a martial arts revenge actioner set during Korea’s Joseon era, with Jung Woo-sung and “Squid Game” star Wi Ha-jun.

	“The Hit List” adapts a Kakao webtoon that has drawn more than 120 million views. The story follows Han Myeong-hoe, among the most powerful men of the Joseon era, who climbed to the top through bloodshed. Opposite him is Baek E-hwa, a woman who loses everything to Han and turns her life over to revenge. Han’s right-hand man, Jang Gil-do, is a fearsome warrior in his own right.
	

	Jung, whose credits include “12.12: The Day,” “Hunt,” “A Man of Reason” and “The Good, the Bad, the Weird,” plays Han. Wi, known for the “Squid Game” series, plays Grand Prince Suyang, who relies on Han’s support in his bid to take the throne from his young nephew.

	Two of Kim’s “Gangs of London” collaborators have followed him to the set. Lars Cox, who has worked on HBO’s “House of the Dragon” and Netflix’s “The Witcher,” is director of photography. Gaffer Kieran Waites, who has worked on Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and the “Fast & Furious” films, has also joined.

	South Korean sales company Finecut unveiled the project. It said the film pairs Korean storytelling with international production know-how, particularly for its big action scenes and period world. “The Hit List” is Finecut’s second project with Kim after “Project Wolf Hunting.”
	

	Kim’s earlier genre work includes “Traffickers” (2012), “The Con Artists” (2014), “The Chase” (2017) and “Metamorphosis” (2019). “Project Wolf Hunting” (2022) bowed in the Midnight section of the Toronto International Film Festival. It then played Sitges, Brussels and other festivals and was distributed in more than 70 countries. Kim later signed with WME, the agency that represents Park Chan-wook and Bong Joon Ho.

	Cheum Film, Studio Take, Library Company and B&C Group are producing, and Mascot Company is presenting. Cameras started rolling in October.

schema.headline: ‘Gangs of London’ Director Kim Hong-sun Shoots Korean Martial Arts Action Film ‘The Hit List’ With Jung Woo-sung, ‘Squid Game’ Star Wi Ha-jun

title: K-Pop Concert Film ‘Twice: This Is For… You’ Acquired by Bleecker Street’s Crosswalk and Universal Pictures International
description: Bleecker Street’s event cinema division Crosswalk and Universal Pictures Content Group have acquired North American and international rights, respe
body:
Bleecker Street’s event cinema division Crosswalk and Universal Pictures Content Group have acquired North American and international rights, respectively, to “Twice: This Is For… You.”

	The film captures K-pop phenomenon Twice at London’s O2 Arena during their “This Is For” world tour. It features concert footage and exclusive behind-the-scenes access to the group.

	“Twice are a truly global phenomenon, and ‘This Is For… You’ ‘captures everything that makes their live performances so special,” said Helen Parker, executive vice president of Universal Pictures Content Group. 
	

	This release builds on the success of “Stray Kids: The dominATE Experience” concert film featuring the global K-pop group Stray Kids, which Crosswalk and Universal Pictures Content Group distributed earlier this year. Paul Dugdale, who directed the film, directed “Twice: This Is For… You.”

	“Following the incredible response to ‘Stray Kids: The dominATE Experience,’ we’re delighted to continue our partnership with Crosswalk and Live Nation to bring another world-class K-pop experience to cinemas and give fans around the world the opportunity to experience it together on the big screen,” Parker added.

	Dugdale (“Stray Kids: The dominATE Experience,” “Adele: One Night Only,” “Taylor Swift: Reputation Stadium Tour”) and Hannah Lux Davis (ADELA’s “Nicole Kidman” and Ariana Grande’s “thank you, next”) directed the film. The film is produced by Live Nation Studios. Crosswalk will release the film in the U.S. and Canada, and Universal Pictures International across international territories.
	

	Twice is a nine-member K-pop group consisting of Nayeon, Jeongyeon, Momo, Sana, Jihyo, Mina, Dahyun, Chaeyoung and Tzuyu. The group formed under JYP Entertainment in 2015 and is one of the best-selling K-pop recording artists of all time, with a No. 1 hit on the Billboard 200, seven consecutive top 10 entries on the chart and two Gold and one Platinum certification from the RIAA.

	“Twice: This Is For… You” is set for theatrical release on Feb. 5, 2027.

schema.headline: K-Pop Concert Film ‘Twice: This Is For… You’ Acquired by Bleecker Street’s Crosswalk and Universal Pictures International

title: Microdrama Makers From Turkey and Japan Bet on Emotional Hooks and Infuriating Villains at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
description: Microdramas compete for attention in crowded mobile feeds, but a strong opening hook does not always need a dramatic twist, İlkin Kavukcu, founder
body:
Microdramas compete for attention in crowded mobile feeds, but a strong opening hook does not always need a dramatic twist, İlkin Kavukcu, founder and CEO of Turkish studio İki Dakika Creative House, said at a Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) session on microdramas in Taipei.

	Kavukcu said her studio looks for moments of emotional recognition that might prompt viewers to stop scrolling and see something of their own lives in a story. Audience sharing, she said, is one sign that a series has connected. İki Dakika distributes its work on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, aiming to build longer-running stories around characters rather than relying on a succession of one-off plot twists.
	

	Kavukcu also described a business model that brings brands into the creation of a story world, giving them a role in shaping the fictional world and its economic model rather than simply placing a product in an episode. İki Dakika has worked with around 30 local and global brands, she said, and is developing co-productions with Italy, a choice she linked to shared cultural themes such as family and tradition.

	Sawamura Naomichi, CEO of emole Inc. and founder of Japanese short-form drama platform Bump, outlined four popular genres in Japan: female rivalries, hidden identities, infidelity and revenge, and lightly suggestive dramas aimed at men. Female rivalry stories, he said, depend on sharp dialogue and characters who may be easy to mock but remain endearing enough to win viewers’ support. Sawamura said the genre also resonates in Taiwan and South Korea, while hidden-identity stories have wider international appeal.
	

	He said the hidden-identity format keeps viewers watching by delaying a protagonist’s reveal and the moment they confront their antagonists. Infidelity and revenge, meanwhile, can establish a relationship and its central betrayal quickly, giving viewers an immediate reason to hope the protagonist will retaliate. That speed suits a format with little time for extended setup, Sawamura said.

	For Bump, the first episode is critical, Sawamura said. The company tracks audience drop-off in the first 30 seconds and whether viewers move on to Episode 2. A strong opening should establish the protagonist’s emotional stakes, the central conflict and the payoff viewers can anticipate. Making the villain’s behavior sufficiently infuriating can build the audience’s desire to see them punished, he said.

	Bump typically spends about two months developing a project before script approval, followed by roughly 30 days for filming and post-production, Sawamura said. A 25-episode series with about 45 minutes of total runtime can be filmed in four days, and the company currently has 20 to 30 projects in production at once.

	Asked whether microdrama IP can extend into other formats, Kavukcu said, “We are already doing this. We can shoot in both vertical and horizontal formats, as long as we have a long enough production schedule. In Turkey, companies including Disney are also interested in trying this.”

	Sawamura said Bump already has examples of IP being developed further, with manga and animation particularly well suited. “Gundam represents a market worth JPY500 billion to JPY600 billion [$3.2 billion to $3.8 billion],” he said, referring to Bandai Namco’s giant-robot franchise. “Since an app like ours is similar to a manga app, we can consider adapting microdramas into manga or animation.”

	Bump has also tested co-productions in the U.S. and South Korea. Sawamura said local partners helped shape scripts around cultural context, relatable relationships and social media trends. Company information provided for the session says Bump has surpassed 4 million downloads, with more than 7 billion social media views.

schema.headline: Microdrama Makers From Turkey and Japan Bet on Emotional Hooks and Infuriating Villains at Taiwan Creative Content Fest

title: Trump on ’60 Minutes’ Reflects on Midterm Loss, Death and Forgiveness: ‘I Do Hate Some of My Enemies’
description: President Trump told “60 Minutes” that he blames Republican candidates and the war in Iran for the party’s midterm defeat, and acknowledged that hi
body:
President Trump told “60 Minutes” that he blames Republican candidates and the war in Iran for the party’s midterm defeat, and acknowledged that his mass deportation policy was “too tough.”

	Sitting down with correspondent Ross Douthat, Trump was also asked about corruption, UFOs and his views of the afterlife. Douthat, a Catholic conservative, asked Trump whether he could forgive enemies like James Comey and Nancy Pelosi as a condition of getting into heaven.
	

	Trump responded that they are “very bad people” and “very dishonest” and said that pretending to forgive them would mean that he wasn’t being “real.”

	“You are telling me you couldn’t find it in your heart to forgive some of your enemies, after all that’s been given to you?” Douthat asked.

	“Can I be honest?” Trump said. “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will.”

	Nevertheless, Trump suggested he may work with Democrats on an immigration bill next year, and appeared open to the idea that his administration had been too punitive in its deportation policy.

	“It was too tough,” he said. “I think it might be too tough.”

	Shortly after the Friday interview, however, he elevated immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to the position of chief of staff.

	Asked about the reasons for Republicans’ resounding defeat, Trump echoed the conventional wisdom that it was about the Iran war and gas prices, but also cited hostility to Israel as a factor.

	“They didn’t like the war,” Trump said. “They didn’t like the fact that gasoline went up because I had it down at a low. And there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.”
	

	He also suggested that Israel would have to “pay us back” for the costs of the war. “Without us, Israel wouldn’t exist,” he said. “Israel would not exist except for Donald Trump.”

	Trump said, however, that he would do the Iran war all over again, and did not signal a major change in course as a result of the election on any other issues. “I’ve had the best two years in the history of the presidency,” he said.

	Douthat, who was hired away from the New York Times in July, got mixed results as he explored metaphysical subjects with the president.

	“What do you think happens when you die?” Douthat asked. “I hope I’m missed,” Trump replied.

	Trump also described himself as a “religious person” and said he hopes to go to heaven.

	Trump deflected questions about his massive increase in wealth since returning to the White House, saying that his son runs his company and that he is unaware of his net worth. “I guess it’s gone up,” he said. “I don’t even know.”

schema.headline: Trump on ’60 Minutes’ Reflects on Midterm Loss, Death and Forgiveness: ‘I Do Hate Some of My Enemies’

title: ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Dazzling Cast Can’t Elevate the Musical’s Muted Narrative
description: One of the most beautiful things about legends and myths is they often stem from the truth. Written by playwright and lyricist Angelica Chéri and d
body:
One of the most beautiful things about legends and myths is they often stem from the truth. Written by playwright and lyricist Angelica Chéri and directed by Stevie Walker-Webb, the new Broadway musical “Wanted” is inspired by Chéri’s great-great aunts, Mary (Solea Pfeiffer) and Martha Clarke (Liisi LaFontaine). These Black women living in post-emancipation Texas decided to pass for white and wield their beauty and guns to save their family’s land and legacy. Unfortunately, despite the exceptional performances and vocal talent, the play’s actual narrative isn’t as compelling as it could be.
	

	According to the Kinfolk, the ensemble that leads the audience into the story, this tale begins in 1893 in Marlon, Texas, in the middle of a cotton field. After struggling and saving with their mother, Tallulah (a phenomenal Ledisi), sharecroppers Mary and Martha are eager to finally buy the land the Clarke family has worked on for generations. However, the landowner, Mr. Billingsley (Nathan Quay Thomas), has other plans. Fueled by racist fury when the women offer a sum of $200 for ownership of the property, he snaps. Rejecting their hard-earned money, he claims the Clarkes are behind on rent and demands double, or he’ll evict them.

	With little recourse beyond their pale skin, courtesy of their long-vanished French father, Mary and Martha set out together beyond Marlon’s country roads to earn money and save themselves and their mother from destitution. Yet as single women traipsing around the 19th-century American South, they become an immediate target. Armed with Ole Bessie, Tallulah’s pistol, the sisters soon discover that stealing and intimidation earn them cash much faster than any other profession. Though their criminality affords them more than they ever hoped, their carefully laid plans are thwarted when they stumble upon a saloon owned by the infamous Jesse Banks (Bradley Jaden), who immediately sets his sights on Mary.
	

	Yet the Clarke sisters aren’t really the outlaws the play tried to make them out to be. Aside from a couple of stick-ups and some seducing and scheming, the rebel storyline fizzles before it even really gets started. Instead, Mary finds herself enamored with Jesse, a wealthy white man who has no idea she is a Black woman. Meanwhile, Martha reluctantly finds herself charmed by Elijah (Luke James), a Black man employed by Jesse. Only through their relationships with these different men does the conflict between the sisters arise, making the story less intriguing and more par for the course.

	Though the narrative isn’t particularly distinct, especially since the central plot largely focuses on the sisters finding love rather than their outlaw status or the true costs of passing, the show’s vocal talent is beyond exceptional. Ledisi, LaFontaine and Pfeiffer are all phenomenal. Backed by an orchestra led by Paul Byssainthe, Jr., the play has several standout numbers, including “Inheritance” and “Mary’s Nightmare.” But the rest of the musical numbers and lyrics don’t exactly pack a punch. Scenic design by Beowulf Boritt and video and projection design by Stefania Bulbarella give the stage much-needed depth, allowing the audience to understand the texture of the time period and place. The singing itself, though, is truly the glue that holds the entire show together. 

	Though passing as an act of defiance and self-preservation is certainly interesting, these themes have been explored to a fault in films like 1934 and 1959’s “Imitation of Life” and books like Brit Bennett’s “The Vanishing Half” and Nella Larsen’s “Passing.” Unfortunately, what Mary experiences isn’t a new or refreshing take on the subject. Instead, “Wanted” presents her as dangerously naive and bewilderingly selfish, far from the badass criminal she’s initially depicted as.

	In the end, because of its overstuffed book and themes, “Wanted” doesn’t quite know what it’s about, resulting in an underwhelming account of who the Clarke sisters were and why their story stands out in American history. Lacking true focus and direction, and leaning heavily on a rushed love story, “Wanted” works best as a musical album. As a Broadway show, however, it simply doesn’t measure up.

schema.headline: ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Dazzling Cast Can’t Elevate the Musical’s Muted Narrative

title: Remembering Sebastián Lelio, an Auteur Who Centered Women’s Stories With Style and Sensitivity
description: When it was announced, in 2017, that the Chilean writer-director Sébastian Lelio was to helm a U.S. remake of his 2013 breakout film “Gloria,” admi
body:
When it was announced, in 2017, that the Chilean writer-director Sébastian Lelio was to helm a U.S. remake of his 2013 breakout film “Gloria,” admirers of the original — and indeed of Lelio himself — had cause for concern. English-language do-overs of world cinema successes frequently go awry; furthermore, we had the cautionary tale of Dutchman George Sluizer, who directed a hopeless 1993 remake of his own impeccable 1988 chiller “The Vanishing,” to remind us that even having the original filmmaker in charge was no guarantee against a travesty.
	

	The news came at a crucial moment in Lelio’s career. The first of his two films to premiere in 2017, the vibrant, heartfelt transgender character study “A Fantastic Woman,” was riding a wave of festival and critical success that began with a Best Screenplay win at the Berlinale, and culminated with an Oscar for Best International Feature (or Best Foreign Language Film, as the award was still called then) — the first ever win for a Chilean film in the category, sealing a resurgence of the country’s cinema also being led by such contemporaries as Sebastián Silva and Lelio’s own producer Pablo Larraín.

	The second, “Disobedience,” was Lelio’s English-language debut — another story of queer identity, but an altogether different tonal and stylistic proposition. A sober portrayal of an illicit romance between two women from North London’s strict Orthodox Jewish community, it was sensitively observed and beautifully acted by leads Rachel Weisz and Rachel McAdams, with a restraint that was occasionally countered by moments of frank, charged sensuality. The contrast between “A Fantastic Woman” and “Disobedience” confirmed Lelio as a particularly empathetic and versatile teller of women’s stories — and “Gloria,” a warm and unsentimentally joyous comedy of a fiftysomething divorcée’s reawakening, was also a good one. But why go back, when his career was barreling forward?
	

	As it turned out, Lelio knew better than his doubters. The remake, which eventually premiered in 2019 as “Gloria Bell,” hewed close to the template of the original, largely inheriting its pleasures and poignancies. But if that makes it sound redundant, it proved a canny and fascinating exercise in performer-as-auteur influence: It was clear that Lelio, self-evidently a champion of women on screen, was interested to see how a wholly different actress would change the tone and temperature of his original story. 

	A lot, we learned. Paulina García was a funny and resilient force of nature in the 2013 original; in “Gloria Bell,” Julianne Moore brought a yearning, lonely fragility to the material that gave even the film’s uplifting trajectory an undertow of melancholy. The remake got less than its due — Moore, at the very least, deserved some awards attention that year — but it sits beside “Gloria” as an illuminating companion piece rather than a competing interpretation.

	I lead with the two Glorias because their respective successes improbably prove a truth about Lelio, a restlessly curious and compassionate filmmaker who passed away, far too soon, on Friday, aged just 52: Even when ostensibly making the same film twice, he never made the same film twice.

	His 2005 debut “The Sacred Family” was confident and a bit scrappy, its handheld jaggedness far removed from his later polish, its droll comic tale of a bourgeois man falling for his son’s girlfriend also distinct from the searching feminist portraiture that would define his later career. But it was lively and promising, made in a semi-improvised fashion that he carried forward into his next, more complex film, the troubled youth study “Navidad,” which made its way into the 2009 Cannes Directors’ Fortnight program. But his third film, 2011’s “The Year of the Tiger,” was a considerably more sophisticated effort: an exquisitely understated exploration of faith, guilt and trauma in the wake of Chile’s devastating 2010 earthquake.

	“The Year of the Tiger,” which competed at Locarno, was too soulful and richly considered a work on its own terms to be seen as a bid for arthouse-major status — but that’s how it worked out anyway, even if the film didn’t get quite the global exposure it deserved. But by the time “Gloria” came along two years later, the word on Lelio was out and expectations were high: The film was selected for the main competition at Berlin and was an immediate, ebulliently received crowdpleaser. If Larraín had established himself as the dark prince of new Chilean cinema with spiky, perverse, politically bristling works like “Post Mortem” and “No,” Lelio was poised to become its great humanist: his touch light but not soft, his perspective probing but not abrasive.
	

	“A Fantastic Woman,” four years later, delivered on that promise. Propelled by trans star Daniela Vega’s extraordinary, emotionally unguarded performance, its story of a grieving trans woman spurned by the prejudiced family of her dead lover arrived at a vital tipping point for the visibility of transgender narratives and artists in popular culture, and delicately essayed an arc of emphatic, even triumphant self-definition amid a climate of isolation and rejection — all without feeling glibly or opportunistically issue-driven. It was to Lelio’s credit that he was fairly self-effacing in his promotion of the film, letting Vega — with whom he had closely developed the protagonist, aligned with her experience — be its chief ambassador and spokesperson. 

	“A Fantastic Woman” earned Lelio the most acclaim and kudos of his career — though his finest film as a director, to my mind, was comparatively shortchanged. A period drama set in 19th-century Ireland and adapted from a novel by “Room” author Emma Donoghue, “The Wonder” didn’t outwardly look or feel much like a Lelio joint — with its austerely repressed milieu shot, by Ari Wegner, with such a damp, chilly verdigris finish you could practically sense moss growing on the screen as you watched. Yet its story of feminine resolve and dueling moral and spiritual convictions meshed well with the director’s interests, as did Florence Pugh’s tenacious, stout-hearted performance; the film’s earthy folktale trappings stood in exciting contrast to its stark formalist construction.

	If “The Wonder” was an ambitious and grandly realized reach, I was less sold on the huge stylistic swing of Lelio’s most recent film, last year’s political musical “The Wave,” which returned him to his homeland. Inspired by a national spate of #MeToo-related feminist student protests that shut down universities across Chile in 2018, it was rhetorically heavy-handed but composed and choreographed with dynamic aplomb, positively thrilling to the spectacle of massed bodies in motion: I wrote in my review that it made one eager to see Lelio tackle more musical fare on screen, never thinking that the film would be his last.

	In one of “The Wave’s” more playful flourishes, the fourth wall is broken to acknowledge Lelio’s own presence as the director of the movie — and to ask, pointedly, what a male director was doing on this expressly feminist project anyway. It’s a wink-wink joke that more seriously encapsulated the generous, conscientious, community-minded approach that Lelio brought to his filmmaking: His auteur signature was subtly distinctive, yet he never made himself the star of his work.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Admits Affair, Company Probing Alleged Chinese Recruitment Plot, Report
description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
                          Admits Affair, Company Probes Alleged Spy Plot
body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
                          Admits Affair, Company Probes Alleged Spy Plot
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Nvidia's married CEO Jensen Huang has openly admitted to an affair, leading to a probe by his company into an alleged foreign recruitment plot ... according to a bombshell report.
      
    
            Jensen -- who is married to Lori Huang -- made the startling admission to employees in an internal message obtained by the Financial Times.
      
    
            The exec apparently wrote ... "I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
      

            While he didn't name the person he had an affair with ... the Financial Times reported that top US officials claimed Jensen had a romantic relationship with a woman named Alice Huang that U.S. intelligence believed was a Chinese spy.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Both the Financial Times and New York Times cite Alice as the person listed in a classified memo alleging she was a possible recruit of the Chinese Ministry of State Security.
      
    
            Alice is an exec at Megaspeed -- which did business with Nvidia. Before his apology ... Jensen told Bloomberg News in October that his interactions with her were "related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual."
      
    
            Following Jensen's internal message about the affair ... Nvidia's board said they would begin an independent probe "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
      
    
            The board added in their statement ... "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information."
      
    
            We've reached out to Megaspeed AI for comment on Alice's behalf ... so far, no word back.

            Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss proved their past rumored feud is way behind them ... as the two Squad members were seen all smiles at the Kansas City Chiefs game.
      
    
            The pop star and her supermodel friend were spotted in a box at Arrowhead Stadium Sunday ... with Karlie bringing her son Levi -- whom she shares husband Joshua Kushner -- in tow!
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Not only that, but Taylor's mom Andrea and dad Scott also showed up to root for their son-in-law! With this many close friends and family members, it's basically a reunion of Taylor and Travis Kelce's wedding.
      

            Speaking of ... Karlie managed to snag an invite to the nuptials after years of not being seen with the singer amid a rumored fallout that began around 2017 or 2018. Now that they're hanging, there's no doubt that their issues -- which we were told were real -- are a thing of the past.
      
    
            Taylor is there to root for Travis and the rest of the Chiefs as they take on the New York Jets -- this after the Big Apple's other team, the Knicks, showed their support for the singer after point guard Tyler Kolek called her "a little performative."
      
    
            The last one of Travis' games Taylor attended was back in October ... where she went from performing in L.A. to cheering in the stands in less than 24 hours.
